summary: Defines a common terminology for GMPLS-based recovery mechanisms, meaning protection and restoration. The terminology does not depend on the underlying transport technology. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A glossary so everybody uses the same words when they talk about backup paths in a network.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary for backup paths, failure handling and switch-over in GMPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Protection and restoration of label switched paths in GMPLS networks were described with inconsistent words drawn from many sources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one set of terms, independent of the transport technology and borrowed from ITU-T G.808.1 and G.841: traffic types, recovery types such as 1+1 and 1:N, bridges and selectors, recovery phases and timings.
tldr.outcome: Other GMPLS recovery documents can use the same terms. The RFC defines terminology only and specifies no protocol.

today: RFC 4427 is an Informational RFC from March 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines terms only; related GMPLS recovery documents include RFC 4426 and RFC 4428.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4427 defines a common terminology for recovery in networks controlled by Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). In this document recovery covers both protection and restoration, and the narrower words are used only when the difference matters. The terminology is independent of the underlying transport technology and borrows from the ITU-T recommendations G.808.1 and G.841.

It focuses on recovery of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) and applies to end-to-end, segment and span (link) recovery. Recovery of the control plane itself is out of scope. Recovery typically means activating a recovery LSP when the working LSP fails, and the two paths are typically resource disjoint so one failure does not hit both.
sections.plainLanguage: A working path carries your traffic. A recovery path is the spare. This document is the dictionary for talking about the spare.

sections.title: Core Concepts: Traffic, Protection and Restoration
sections.content:
A working LSP carries normal user traffic. A recovery LSP carries that traffic when the working LSP fails and may carry extra traffic (pre-emptable traffic) while idle. Three traffic types are defined: normal traffic, extra traffic (not protected by definition, pre-empted when the recovery resources are needed) and null traffic (carried when nothing else uses the recovery LSP, and ignored at its egress).

The difference between protection and restoration is how much of the recovery path exists before a failure. In protection, route computation is done, the LSP is fully signaled and its resources are cross-connected end to end, so no signaling is needed to set it up after a failure. In restoration, some resources may be pre-computed, signaled and selected, but the path is not cross-connected, so full establishment happens only after the failure and needs extra signaling. Both need signaling of some kind.

Recovery can be applied to a span (a link between two nodes), to a segment of an end-to-end LSP, or to the whole LSP from ingress to egress. A recovery domain is the set of nodes and spans covered by one or more recovery schemes and must lie entirely inside a GMPLS domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Protection is like keeping a spare tire already mounted and ready. Restoration is like having a spare in the trunk that you fit only after the flat.

sections.title: Recovery Types, Bridges and Selectors
sections.content:
Recovery types are classified by how many recovery LSPs protect how many working LSPs. In 1+1, one dedicated protection LSP protects one working LSP and the normal traffic is permanently duplicated at the ingress, so no extra traffic is possible. In 1:1, traffic goes over one LSP at a time and the spare can carry extra traffic. In 1:N, one recovery LSP serves up to N working LSPs, and in M:N, M recovery LSPs serve up to N working LSPs. For the shared types all LSPs must start and end at the same nodes, and if more fail at once only one (or M) can be recovered. 0:1 means no specific recovery LSP exists and the working LSP can only be restored over some alternate route.

The bridge connects normal and extra traffic to the working and recovery LSPs. A permanent bridge (1+1) feeds both LSPs, a broadcast bridge (1:N, M:N) adds the recovery LSP only on switching, and a selector bridge connects traffic to one or the other. The selector at the egress extracts normal traffic from the working or recovery output; a merging selector reads both and works only with a selector bridge.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge is the switch that decides which road the cars enter, and a selector is the gate at the far end that decides which road the cars leave from.

sections.title: Recovery Phases and Timing
sections.content:
The RFC lists five generic phases when an LSP, span or node fails: failure detection, failure localization (and isolation), failure notification, recovery (protection or restoration) and reversion (normalization). Detection is the only phase the control plane cannot do alone. Detection, localization and notification together are called fault management.

Four kinds of entity take part: a detecting entity, a reporting entity that correlates failures, a deciding entity that picks the recovery resources, and a recovering entity. For span recovery the deciding and recovering node is the master and the other end node is the slave.

Timing terms are detection time, correlation time, notification time and recovery switching time. Their sum is the total recovery time. The wait to restore time is how long must pass after a recovered fault before the LSP is reused. Failure signals include Signal Degrade (SD) and Signal Fail (SF), with group variants SDG and SFG.
sections.plainLanguage: When something breaks, someone notices, someone finds where, someone tells the right people, someone switches traffic, and later the traffic goes back. Each step has a name and a timer.

sections.title: Reversion, Switching Modes and Operator Commands
sections.content:
Reversion decides what happens once the working path is healthy. In a revertive operation traffic returns to, or stays on, the working LSP when the switch-over requests end. In a non-revertive operation it does not return. Switching can be unidirectional, moving only the affected direction, or bi-directional, moving both directions after a one-direction fault.

Operators can also influence recovery through the management system with external commands: lockout of the recovery LSP, lockout of normal traffic, freeze, forced switch-over, manual switch-over for normal traffic, manual switch-over for the recovery LSP, and clear. Forced and manual switch-overs respect any equal or higher priority command in effect.

Other defined terms include full versus partial span recovery, impairment, recovery ratio, hitless protection switch-over (no loss, duplication, disorder or bit errors), network survivability and escalation.
sections.plainLanguage: After a road reopens, a rule says whether traffic goes back to it. Operators can also press buttons to force a switch, freeze everything, or block the spare.

sections.title: Protection and Restoration Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC then names concrete schemes. Protection schemes are 1+1 (permanent bridge, receiver picks the better of the two LSPs), 1:N and M:N (shared protection that may carry unprotected extra traffic). All protection types except 1+1 unidirectional switching need a communication channel between ingress and egress.

Restoration schemes are pre-planned LSP restoration (also called re-routing), where restoration LSPs are pre-computed and signaled but not cross-connected, and LSP restoration, where the path is signaled and fully established after the failure and may be computed after it (full LSP re-routing). Shared-mesh restoration lets restoration LSPs from distinct ingress nodes share resources. Hard restoration releases the old LSP before the new one is fully up (break-before-make); soft restoration releases it afterward (make-before-break).

For security, the RFC points to RFC 4428 and RFC 4426.
sections.plainLanguage: A pre-built spare road, a spare road paved only after the crash, and the choice between closing the old road first or after the new one opens.

items.label: Dedicated protection
items.desc: One protection LSP/span per working LSP/span, traffic permanently duplicated, no extra traffic.

items.label: Unprotected
items.desc: No specific recovery LSP; the working LSP can only be restored over an alternate route.

items.label: Dedicated recovery with extra traffic
items.desc: One recovery LSP per working LSP, traffic on one at a time.

items.label: Shared recovery with extra traffic
items.desc: One recovery LSP protects up to N working LSPs.

items.label: Shared set
items.desc: M recovery LSPs protect up to N working LSPs, with N >= M.

cells: Some signaled in advance, more after failure
